questions.stem:
A 42-year-old man has had 1 day of abrupt fever, chills, muscle aches, headache, and cough in January. A rapid molecular test of a nasal swab is positive for influenza A. He is prescribed an oral drug twice daily for 5 days. In cell culture, the drug does not stop the virus from entering cells or copying its genome, but newly made virions remain stuck to the surface of the infected cell.

Which viral protein does this drug inhibit?
choices: Hemagglutinin, which attaches the virus to host cells
Neuraminidase, which cleaves sialic acid to release progeny virus
Polymerase acidic protein, which has endonuclease activity
Thymidine kinase, which phosphorylates nucleoside analogs
DNA terminase complex, which packages new viral genomes

explain.html:
Influenza uses two surface proteins at opposite ends of its life cycle: hemagglutinin attaches the virus to the host cell, and neuraminidase cleaves sialic acid from glycoproteins so newly made virions can leave the cell. The neuraminidase inhibitors (oseltamivir by mouth, zanamivir by inhalation, peramivir intravenously) block that last step and so prevent release of virus from infected cells. Entry and genome copying proceed normally, but progeny stay tethered to the cell surface and cannot spread. They act on influenza A and B, and resistance comes from mutations in neuraminidase, more often in influenza A.

In this vignette the drug is oral and given twice daily for 5 days, the treatment course of oseltamivir, and the culture result (entry and replication intact, virions stuck on the surface) is the signature of neuraminidase blockade. Knowing which step each influenza drug hits lets you predict what a lab assay will show and why a resistant strain escapes.
explain.table:
Influenza drugTargetStep blockedRoute
OseltamivirNeuraminidaseRelease of progeny virusOral, twice daily for 5 days
ZanamivirNeuraminidaseRelease of progeny virusInhaled
PeramivirNeuraminidaseRelease of progeny virusIV, one dose
BaloxavirPolymerase acidic endonucleaseTranscription, so replicationOral, one dose
why: Hemagglutinin mediates attachment, and the drug left viral entry untouched.
The polymerase acidic endonuclease is baloxavir's target, and blocking it would stop genome transcription, which proceeded here.
Thymidine kinase is the herpesvirus enzyme that activates acyclovir; influenza has no role for it.
The DNA terminase complex is a cytomegalovirus target of letermovir, and influenza is an RNA virus.
explain.takeaway: Neuraminidase inhibitors (oseltamivir, zanamivir, peramivir) block cleavage of sialic acid, so influenza A and B virions cannot be released from infected cells.
explain.subject: Pharmacology
explain.objective: Explain pharmacology of antiviral and antifungal agents

rows.if_right: a drug that kept influenza from attaching to and entering host cells

questions.stem:
A 28-year-old woman with moderate persistent asthma develops influenza B. She is started on an inhaled antiviral twice daily. Within an hour of the second dose she has chest tightness and wheezing, and her peak flow drops by 30%. Her asthma had been well controlled.

Which antiviral would be the better choice for her?
choices: Inhaled zanamivir at a lower dose
Oral acyclovir
Intravenous foscarnet
Oral valganciclovir
Oral oseltamivir

explain.html:
The three neuraminidase inhibitors share a mechanism and a class adverse effect profile (insomnia, vertigo, neuropsychiatric events, most often with oseltamivir), but each has a unique adverse effect tied to how it is given. Zanamivir is inhaled, and its unique adverse effect is bronchospasm; peramivir, given IV, instead carries hyperglycemia, liver enzyme or CPK elevations and SJS. The route, not the target, drives the airway toxicity. This patient has asthma, took the inhaled drug, and within an hour had wheezing and a 30% fall in peak flow, which is zanamivir bronchospasm.

The fix is to keep the mechanism and change the route: oral oseltamivir inhibits neuraminidase and covers influenza A and B without delivering drug to reactive airways. The remaining options are herpesvirus drugs with no activity against influenza.
explain.table:
Neuraminidase inhibitorRouteUnique adverse effect
OseltamivirOralNeuropsychiatric events most likely (shared class effect)
ZanamivirInhaledBronchospasm
PeramivirIVHyperglycemia, liver enzyme or CPK elevation, SJS
why: A lower dose still delivers zanamivir to her airways, which is what triggered the bronchospasm.
Acyclovir treats herpes simplex and varicella zoster virus, not influenza.
Foscarnet is reserved for resistant cytomegalovirus and herpesvirus infections and does not treat influenza.
Valganciclovir is an oral cytomegalovirus drug with no influenza activity.
explain.takeaway: Inhaled zanamivir uniquely causes bronchospasm, so patients with asthma should receive oral oseltamivir, which has the same neuraminidase mechanism.

explain.objective: List adverse effects for specific agents

questions.stem:
A 17-year-old boy with uncomplicated influenza A is given a single oral dose of an antiviral. The prodrug is converted to an active form that inhibits the endonuclease activity of a selective polymerase acidic protein that the virus needs for transcription. He swallows the tablet with a large glass of milk and an antacid for an upset stomach.

Which of the following is the most likely consequence of how he took the dose?
choices: Bronchospasm from airway delivery
Increased conversion to the active drug
Nephrotoxicity from crystal formation
Reduced drug absorption
Visual disturbances and hallucinations

explain.html:
Baloxavir marboxil is a prodrug converted to baloxavir, which inhibits the endonuclease activity of the polymerase acidic protein that influenza A and B need for transcription, so viral replication stops. Its half-life of about 79 hours is why it is given orally as a single dose, approved for uncomplicated influenza or post-exposure prophylaxis in patients older than 12. Adverse effects are mild (diarrhea, nasopharyngitis).

The pharmacokinetic catch is that its absorption is affected by dairy products and cations. This teenager swallowed his one tablet with milk and an antacid, so less drug reaches the blood, and with only one dose there is no later dose to make up the shortfall. When a drug is given once, anything that lowers absorption threatens the whole course, so counsel patients to separate it from dairy and cation-containing products.
why: Bronchospasm comes from airway delivery of inhaled zanamivir, and baloxavir is swallowed.
Milk and antacids do not speed conversion of the prodrug; they lower how much is absorbed.
Nephrotoxicity is a concern with IV acyclovir, cidofovir and foscarnet, not baloxavir.
Visual hallucinations are the unique adverse effect of voriconazole, an antifungal.
explain.takeaway: Baloxavir, a single-dose oral inhibitor of the influenza polymerase acidic endonuclease, has reduced absorption when taken with dairy products or cations.
explain.subject: Pharmacology
explain.objective: Explain pharmacology of antiviral and antifungal agents

rows.if_right: an asthmatic patient who inhaled zanamivir

rows.why: Milk and antacids do not speed conversion of the prodrug; they lower how much is absorbed.
rows.if_right: a factor that enhanced hepatic or intestinal activation of a prodrug

rows.if_right: high-dose IV acyclovir or cidofovir given without hydration

rows.if_right: an aspergillosis patient on voriconazole

questions.stem:
A 67-year-old man is admitted with herpes zoster involving multiple dermatomes and is started on high-dose intravenous acyclovir. On day 3 his serum creatinine has risen from 0.9 to 2.3 mg/dL (0.7 to 1.3), and he is newly confused. Once he improves, the team plans to switch him to an oral drug for the rest of the course.

Which oral drug is preferred for the switch, and why?
choices: Oral acyclovir, because it has the highest bioavailability
Valacyclovir, a prodrug giving higher levels
Valganciclovir, because it avoids bone marrow suppression
Oseltamivir, because it does not need renal adjustment
Letermovir, because it does not affect the kidneys at all

explain.html:
Acyclovir and valacyclovir share adverse effects: neurotoxicity, GI upset, myelosuppression, rash and, specifically with IV acyclovir, nephrotoxicity. High-dose IV therapy for multidermatomal zoster therefore explains both his rising creatinine and his new confusion. Once he improves, the oral choice depends on pharmacokinetics. Oral acyclovir has bioavailability of only 15 to 30% and must be dosed many times a day.

Valacyclovir is a prodrug hydrolyzed to acyclovir by first-pass and hepatic metabolism, with oral bioavailability of about 55%. It produces higher serum levels, which also reduces the risk of resistance, and it is more convenient to take, so it is the preferred oral step-down for HSV and VZV. The other options are drugs for different viruses.
explain.table:
DrugRouteOral bioavailabilityKey point
AcyclovirIV or PO15 to 30%Dosed many times a day; IV form nephrotoxic
ValacyclovirPO55%Prodrug, higher levels, less resistance
FamciclovirPO77%Converted to penciclovir
why: Oral acyclovir has the poorest bioavailability (15 to 30%) of the HSV and VZV options, which is why it needs frequent dosing.
Valganciclovir is a cytomegalovirus drug, and myelosuppression is its main adverse effect rather than something it avoids.
Oseltamivir treats influenza and has no activity against varicella zoster virus.
Letermovir is approved only for cytomegalovirus prophylaxis and does not treat zoster.
explain.takeaway: IV acyclovir can cause nephrotoxicity and neurotoxicity; valacyclovir, an acyclovir prodrug with higher bioavailability and serum levels, is the preferred oral agent.

questions.stem:
A 52-year-old man who received a kidney transplant 3 months ago has fever, diarrhea, and rising cytomegalovirus viral load in blood. He is started on an intravenous drug that must be phosphorylated first by a viral kinase encoded by UL97 and then by cellular kinases, after which it is incorporated into viral DNA and terminates chain elongation. Two weeks later his labs are checked.

Which laboratory change is most likely to be found?
choices: Rising absolute neutrophil count
Serum calcium well above the normal range
Very high serum potassium from cell lysis
Isolated rise in hemoglobin
Falling absolute neutrophil and platelet counts

explain.html:
Ganciclovir and its oral prodrug valganciclovir are the drugs of choice for CMV treatment and prophylaxis. Ganciclovir is triphosphorylated to become active, first by the viral kinase encoded by UL97 and then by cellular kinases, and is incorporated during viral DNA synthesis, causing chain termination. Its oral bioavailability is only 5%, so ganciclovir is given IV, while valganciclovir (over 60%) is given by mouth.

The dose-limiting toxicity is myelosuppression, hitting neutrophils and platelets, with anemia also possible; fever, nephrotoxicity and GI effects round out the list. This kidney recipient on IV ganciclovir for two weeks is therefore most likely to show falling neutrophil and platelet counts. Watch for added marrow toxicity with zidovudine or flucytosine, and for seizure risk with imipenem.
explain.table:
CMV drugSignature toxicity
Ganciclovir, valganciclovirMyelosuppression (neutrophils, platelets)
CidofovirNephrotoxicity (give probenecid and saline)
FoscarnetNephrotoxicity, low calcium, potassium, phosphate, magnesium
LetermovirGI, edema; many drug interactions; no marrow toxicity
why: Ganciclovir suppresses the marrow, so the neutrophil count falls rather than rises.
Ganciclovir does not raise calcium, and the CMV drug that disturbs calcium, foscarnet, lowers it.
High potassium is not a ganciclovir effect; foscarnet and amphotericin lower potassium.
Ganciclovir lowers marrow output and can cause anemia, so hemoglobin would not rise in isolation.
explain.takeaway: Ganciclovir (activated first by CMV UL97 kinase) and valganciclovir are first-line for CMV, and their main toxicity is myelosuppression with neutropenia and thrombocytopenia.
explain.subject: Pharmacology
explain.objective: List adverse effects for specific agents

questions.stem:
A 39-year-old man with ganciclovir-resistant cytomegalovirus retinitis is started on intravenous foscarnet. On day 5 he reports tingling around his mouth and in his fingertips, and tapping over the facial nerve causes twitching of the corner of his mouth. Creatinine has risen from 0.8 to 1.6 mg/dL (0.7 to 1.3).

Which laboratory finding best explains his new symptoms?
choices: High serum calcium
Low serum sodium
High serum glucose
Low serum ionized calcium
High serum phosphate

explain.html:
Foscarnet inhibits the pyrophosphate binding site of viral DNA polymerase without needing thymidine kinase or UL97, so it is used for resistant CMV and herpesvirus infections. Its toxicity profile is the price: nephrotoxicity, myelosuppression (anemia) and wasting of electrolytes, producing hypocalcemia, hypokalemia, hypophosphatemia and hypomagnesemia. The low-calcium state shows up as neuromuscular irritability.

This patient's perioral and fingertip tingling and the facial twitch on tapping are signs of low ionized calcium, and his doubling creatinine shows the kidney injury that comes with it. Patients on foscarnet need extra hydration and electrolyte correction, and the dose must be adjusted to kidney function, which is complicated enough that a pharmacist should help.
why: Foscarnet lowers serum calcium rather than raising it, and high calcium would not cause tingling and facial twitching.
Low sodium is not among foscarnet's electrolyte effects, which are calcium, potassium, phosphate and magnesium.
High glucose is not a foscarnet effect; among the antivirals here it is listed for peramivir.
Foscarnet lowers phosphate rather than raising it.
explain.takeaway: Foscarnet causes nephrotoxicity and losses of calcium, potassium, phosphate and magnesium, so perioral tingling and tetany signal hypocalcemia.
explain.subject: Pharmacology
explain.objective: List adverse effects for specific agents

questions.stem:
A 50-year-old man with cytomegalovirus disease resistant to ganciclovir is to start an intravenous nucleotide analog that is converted by cellular enzymes to a diphosphate and incorporated into viral DNA. The drug has a short serum half-life but persists inside cells for a long time. The order set includes more than 1 L of intravenous saline before and during each infusion and an oral drug given with each dose.

The oral drug and the saline are given mainly to reduce which adverse effect?
choices: Bone marrow suppression
Nephrotoxicity
Visual hallucinations
Bronchospasm
Prolonged QT interval

explain.html:
Cidofovir is a nucleotide analog that cellular enzymes convert to cidofovir diphosphate, which incorporates into viral DNA and reduces DNA synthesis. It has a short serum half-life but persists for a long time inside cells. Its major adverse effects are nephrotoxicity and myelosuppression, plus ocular hypotony, uveitis or iritis when given into the eye.

The order set in this stem is built around the kidneys. Probenecid reduces renal excretion of cidofovir, which raises its drug levels and reduces nephrotoxicity, and more than 1 L of fluid before and during the infusion adds protection. When a regimen pairs an antiviral with probenecid and hydration, think cidofovir and renal protection.
explain.table:
Nephrotoxic drugHow the kidney is protected
CidofovirProbenecid plus more than 1 L of fluid
FoscarnetExtra hydration, electrolyte correction, renal dosing
Amphotericin BSaline infusion, liposomal formulation
why: Cidofovir can suppress the marrow, but probenecid and saline are given to protect the kidneys, not the marrow.
Visual hallucinations are the unique adverse effect of voriconazole.
Bronchospasm is the unique adverse effect of inhaled zanamivir.
QT prolongation is an azole class effect and is not what probenecid and fluids prevent.
explain.takeaway: Cidofovir is nephrotoxic, so it is given with probenecid (which reduces its renal excretion and nephrotoxicity) and generous saline hydration.

explain.objective: Explain pharmacology of antiviral and antifungal agents

questions.stem:
A 58-year-old cytomegalovirus-seropositive man is about to undergo an allogeneic stem cell transplant. The team plans to prevent CMV reactivation with a drug that does not inhibit viral DNA polymerase. Instead it targets the viral DNA terminase complex (UL51, UL56, UL89), so new viral DNA is not processed and packaged into virions. Marrow toxicity is a major concern because his graft must engraft.

Which of the following is true of this drug?
choices: It is used for prophylaxis and has many drug interactions
It is mainly used to treat recurrent herpes simplex genital ulcers
It needs phosphorylation by the UL97 kinase to act
It is given by inhalation and can cause bronchospasm
It is used with amphotericin for cryptococcal meningitis

explain.html:
Most CMV drugs act on viral DNA polymerase, but letermovir targets the DNA terminase complex (UL51, UL56, UL89). Without terminase, new viral DNA is not processed into genome-unit lengths or packaged, so virion maturation fails. Because it spares the polymerase pathway, it avoids the myelosuppression that limits ganciclovir, which matters while a stem cell graft engrafts.

Letermovir is approved for prophylaxis, which fits this seropositive transplant candidate. Its adverse effects are GI upset, peripheral edema, fatigue, cough and headache, and it has many drug interactions, including with immunosuppressants, amiodarone, warfarin, phenytoin, voriconazole, statins and rifampin. Any transplant medication list needs review when it starts.
why: Recurrent genital HSV is treated with acyclovir, valacyclovir or famciclovir, not letermovir.
Needing UL97 phosphorylation describes ganciclovir; letermovir acts on terminase without activation.
Inhaled delivery with bronchospasm describes zanamivir for influenza.
Flucytosine, not letermovir, is combined with amphotericin for cryptococcal meningitis.
explain.takeaway: Letermovir inhibits the CMV DNA terminase complex, is approved for prophylaxis, avoids marrow toxicity and has many drug interactions.
explain.subject: Pharmacology
explain.objective: Describe common uses for agents discussed

rows.if_right: a drug activated by viral thymidine kinase for herpes simplex

questions.stem:
A 63-year-old man with leukemia and invasive pulmonary aspergillosis starts an intravenous azole that has nonlinear pharmacokinetics and requires level monitoring. On the second day he reports that colors look abnormally bright and that he saw people standing in his room who were not there. He is oriented and his electrolytes are normal.

Which drug is most likely responsible for his symptoms?
choices: Fluconazole
Isavuconazole
Voriconazole
Micafungin
Flucytosine

explain.html:
The azoles share class adverse effects (elevated liver enzymes, hepatitis, nausea and vomiting, QTc prolongation), but several have a unique effect that identifies them. Voriconazole covers Candida and Aspergillus, has nonlinear pharmacokinetics and is monitored by drug levels (target 2 to 5 mcg/mL), and its unique adverse effect is visual hallucinations and visual disturbance. Isavuconazole also covers Aspergillus, but its unique effect is QTc shortening.

This leukemia patient on an IV azole for pulmonary aspergillosis with level monitoring now sees abnormally bright colors and people who are not there while fully oriented, which is the voriconazole signature. Fluconazole does not cover Aspergillus, and the non-azoles listed have different toxicities. Recognizing the drug prevents a misguided neurologic workup.

AzoleAspergillus?Distinguishing feature
FluconazoleNoCandida only; misses C. glabrata and C. auris
VoriconazoleYesNonlinear kinetics, levels 2 to 5; visual hallucinations
PosaconazoleYesLevel above 1; covers Mucor
IsavuconazoleYesQTc shortening
why: Fluconazole covers Candida, not Aspergillus, and visual hallucinations are not its effect.
Isavuconazole covers Aspergillus, but its unique adverse effect is QTc shortening, not hallucinations.
Micafungin is an echinocandin whose adverse effects are raised liver enzymes and infusion reactions, and it is only salvage therapy for Aspergillus.
Flucytosine is not an azole, does not treat Aspergillus, and mainly causes marrow suppression.
explain.takeaway: Voriconazole treats aspergillosis, requires level monitoring because of nonlinear kinetics, and uniquely causes visual disturbances and hallucinations.

questions.stem:
A 66-year-old man with a long-term urinary catheter has fever, flank pain, and pyuria, and urine culture grows a Candida species. He is started on intravenous micafungin. After 5 days his urine culture remains positive and his symptoms have not improved, even though the isolate is reported as sensitive to micafungin in the laboratory.

Which property of the drug best explains the treatment failure?
choices: Rapid renal clearance before it reaches the bladder wall
Bacterial contamination of the urine sample
Inactivation of the drug by stomach acid
Resistance caused by thymidine kinase loss
Poor penetration into the urinary tract

explain.html:
Laboratory susceptibility only predicts cure if the drug reaches the infected site. Echinocandins such as micafungin are IV only, distribute widely to tissues, and are eliminated mostly by hepatic metabolism. They have no CNS or urinary penetration, so very little active drug appears in the urine.

This catheterized patient with Candida pyelonephritis did not improve on micafungin even though the isolate tested sensitive, which is the predictable consequence of that distribution. The deciding clue is the site (urinary tract), not the organism. Echinocandins are a poor choice for fungal infection of the urine or the CNS, and the antifungal should be picked by where it goes as well as what it kills.
explain.table:
AntifungalRouteEliminationCNS or urine
EchinocandinsIV onlyMostly hepaticNo penetration
Amphotericin BIV onlySlow hepatic; small fraction in urineUsed for cryptococcal meningitis
why: Echinocandins are cleared mostly by the liver, not the kidney, so the problem is that little drug reaches the urine at all.
The culture grew Candida and the patient is symptomatic; the failure is drug delivery, not a contaminated sample.
Micafungin is given IV, so stomach acid cannot inactivate it.
Thymidine kinase loss explains acyclovir resistance in herpes simplex, not antifungal failure.
explain.takeaway: Echinocandins are IV-only, hepatically cleared and do not penetrate the urine or CNS, so they fail in urinary and CNS fungal infections despite in vitro susceptibility.
explain.topic: Echinocandins: no CNS or urinary penetration

explain.objective: Explain pharmacology of antiviral and antifungal agents

questions.stem:
A 34-year-old man with advanced immunosuppression is treated for invasive mold infection with an intravenous antifungal that binds a sterol in the fungal cell membrane. After 10 days his labs are checked.

[[labs 0]]

Which change in therapy would most likely reduce this toxicity while keeping the same drug?
choices: Switching to a liposomal formulation and giving saline
Adding probenecid before each infusion to slow renal excretion
Giving the drug orally instead of intravenously
Adding flucytosine to lower the dose
Pre-medicating with diphenhydramine

explain.html:
An antifungal that binds ergosterol in the cell membrane is amphotericin B, a polyene given only IV. Its nephrotoxic effects are dose-limiting: it lowers the GFR and causes renal tubular acidosis with magnesium and potassium wasting, and anemia can follow from reduced renal erythropoietin production. This patient's labs show all of it (high creatinine, low potassium and magnesium, low bicarbonate, anemia).

To keep the drug and protect the kidney, saline infusion may reduce renal damage, and liposomal formulations have reduced nephrotoxic effects. Pre-medication with diphenhydramine, acetaminophen or an NSAID, and hydrocortisone, with a slower infusion, addresses infusion reactions such as chills and rigors, not kidney injury.
explain.table:
Amphotericin B problemFindingsMitigation
Nephrotoxicity (dose-limiting)Low GFR, RTA, low potassium and magnesium, anemiaSaline loading, liposomal formulation
Infusion reactionFlushing, chills, rigorsDiphenhydramine, acetaminophen or NSAID, hydrocortisone, slow infusion
why: Probenecid is paired with cidofovir to reduce its nephrotoxicity, not with amphotericin.
Amphotericin B is given only intravenously, so there is no oral form to switch to.
Flucytosine is added for cryptococcal meningitis, not to spare the kidney, and it brings its own marrow toxicity.
Diphenhydramine pre-medication prevents infusion reactions such as chills and rigors, not kidney injury.
explain.takeaway: Amphotericin B causes dose-limiting nephrotoxicity (low GFR, RTA with potassium and magnesium wasting, anemia), reduced by saline loading and liposomal formulations.

questions.stem:
A 38-year-old woman receiving chemotherapy has painful, enlarging genital ulcers. Viral PCR of a swab is positive for herpes simplex virus 2. Despite 10 days of high-dose valacyclovir the lesions keep growing. Testing of the isolate shows a mutant virus that lacks the enzyme that normally performs the first phosphorylation of the drug.

Which drug is most appropriate now?
choices: Famciclovir
Ganciclovir
Foscarnet
Penciclovir cream
Oseltamivir

explain.html:
Acyclovir and its prodrug valacyclovir are guanosine analogues that must be activated stepwise: viral thymidine kinase (TK) adds the first phosphate, then human enzymes finish the job to make acyclovir triphosphate. That triphosphate competes for viral DNA polymerase and terminates replication. Resistance comes from viral mutants deficient in TK or with reduced polymerase affinity for acyclovir triphosphate. Famciclovir and penciclovir follow the same route, since penciclovir is also phosphorylated by viral TK.

This immunocompromised patient's HSV-2 lesions grew despite high-dose valacyclovir, and her isolate lacks the enzyme that performs the first phosphorylation, which means every TK-dependent drug is out. Foscarnet inhibits the pyrophosphate binding site of viral DNA polymerase directly and does not require TK for activation, so it still works. Expect its nephrotoxicity and electrolyte losses and plan hydration.
explain.table:
DrugNeeds viral kinase?Still active against TK-deficient HSV?
Acyclovir, valacyclovirYes (viral TK)No
Famciclovir, penciclovirYes (viral TK)No
GanciclovirYes (viral kinase UL97 in CMV)Not the choice
FoscarnetNo, binds polymerase directlyYes
why: Famciclovir is metabolized to penciclovir, which also needs viral TK, so this mutant resists it.
Ganciclovir also depends on viral kinase phosphorylation and is the drug of choice for cytomegalovirus, not TK-deficient HSV.
Penciclovir needs viral TK, and the topical cream is only for oral lesions.
Oseltamivir inhibits influenza neuraminidase and has no activity against herpes simplex.
explain.takeaway: Acyclovir-class drugs need viral thymidine kinase for their first phosphorylation, so TK-deficient herpes simplex is treated with foscarnet, which acts on DNA polymerase without activation.
explain.topic: Acyclovir resistance: thymidine kinase and foscarnet

questions.stem:
A 45-year-old woman 4 months after a stem cell transplant has cytomegalovirus viremia that keeps rising despite 3 weeks of intravenous ganciclovir at the correct dose. Genotyping shows a mutation in the viral gene that encodes the kinase performing the first phosphorylation of ganciclovir; the viral DNA polymerase gene is normal.

Which of the following drugs would still be active against this virus?
choices: Valganciclovir
Valacyclovir
Foscarnet
Famciclovir
Oseltamivir

explain.html:
Ganciclovir must be phosphorylated first by the CMV kinase encoded by UL97 before cellular kinases complete activation. CMV becomes resistant through mutations in UL97 or in UL54, which encodes the viral DNA polymerase. Valganciclovir is simply a prodrug of ganciclovir, so it shares the same resistance mechanisms. A drug that bypasses UL97 is needed when only that gene is mutated.

Foscarnet inhibits the pyrophosphate binding site of viral DNA polymerase directly and needs no viral kinase, so this UL97 mutant with a normal polymerase gene remains sensitive. Cidofovir, a nucleotide analog activated by cellular enzymes, is the other option listed for UL97-mutant CMV. A rising viral load despite correctly dosed ganciclovir should prompt genotyping, because the mutated gene decides which drug still works.
explain.table:
CMV drugActivationUL97 mutant
Ganciclovir, valganciclovirUL97 kinase, then cellular kinasesResistant
CidofovirCellular enzymes to diphosphateActive
FoscarnetNone, binds polymerase directlyActive
LetermovirNone, targets terminaseProphylaxis use
why: Valganciclovir is converted to ganciclovir and shares its UL97 resistance.
Valacyclovir is an acyclovir prodrug for HSV and VZV that also depends on viral kinase activation.
Famciclovir is converted to penciclovir, a viral-kinase-dependent HSV and VZV drug, not a CMV drug.
Oseltamivir targets influenza neuraminidase and has no activity against CMV.
explain.takeaway: CMV resistant to ganciclovir through a UL97 kinase mutation remains sensitive to foscarnet and cidofovir, which do not depend on UL97 for activation.

questions.stem:
A 46-year-old woman who received a liver transplant takes tacrolimus, and her levels have been stable. She develops invasive aspergillosis and starts a drug that inhibits the fungal enzyme that removes a methyl group at position 14 of lanosterol. One week later she has a tremor, and her creatinine has risen from 1.0 to 1.9 mg/dL (0.6 to 1.1). Her tacrolimus trough level is far above target.

Which of the following best explains the rise in tacrolimus level?
choices: The antifungal binds ergosterol and damages the renal tubules
The antifungal inhibits the enzyme that metabolizes tacrolimus
The antifungal displaces tacrolimus from albumin binding sites in blood
The antifungal induces the enzyme that clears tacrolimus
Aspergillus infection directly blocks tacrolimus excretion

explain.html:
Azoles block ergosterol synthesis at the step of 14-alpha demethylation of lanosterol, which disrupts fungal cell membrane permeability. For aspergillosis the azole is usually voriconazole (posaconazole or isavuconazole also cover Aspergillus). The same drugs are CYP3A4 inhibitors, so they cause higher levels of CYP3A4 substrates such as immunosuppressants, warfarin, phenytoin and DOACs.

Here the azole slowed tacrolimus metabolism, and the resulting tacrolimus trough far above target produced tremor and a rising creatinine. The infection did not change tacrolimus handling; the drug interaction did. Any azole started in a transplant patient calls for an interaction check and closer immunosuppressant levels.
explain.table:
Antifungal classMechanismKey interaction or toxicity
AzolesInhibit 14-alpha demethylation of lanosterol (ergosterol synthesis)CYP3A4 inhibition; raise immunosuppressants, warfarin, phenytoin, DOACs
Polyene (amphotericin B)Binds ergosterol in the membraneNephrotoxicity, low potassium and magnesium
EchinocandinsInhibit beta-1,3-glucan synthesis (cell wall)Caspofungin interacts with tacrolimus, cyclosporine
why: Binding ergosterol is the amphotericin B mechanism, not the azole's, and it would not raise tacrolimus levels.
Displacement from albumin is not how azoles interact with tacrolimus; the effect is on its metabolism.
Azoles inhibit CYP3A4; an inducer would lower tacrolimus levels, not raise them.
Aspergillus does not block tacrolimus excretion; the change began with the new drug.
explain.takeaway: Azoles inhibit fungal lanosterol 14-alpha demethylase and also inhibit CYP3A4, raising levels of substrates such as tacrolimus, warfarin and phenytoin.

questions.stem:
A 71-year-old woman in the intensive care unit with a central venous catheter develops fever and hypotension. Blood cultures grow a yeast. She was started on fluconazole, but she remains febrile and cultures stay positive. The laboratory identifies the isolate as Candida glabrata. She has no signs of meningitis or urinary infection.

Which drug class is the best choice now, and how does it act?
choices: Echinocandin; inhibits beta-1,3-glucan synthase in the cell wall
Polyene; inhibits 14-alpha demethylation of lanosterol
Neuraminidase inhibitor; prevents release from infected cells
Antimetabolite; used alone as monotherapy for yeasts
Higher-dose fluconazole; binds ergosterol to form membrane pores

explain.html:
Fluconazole covers most Candida species, but Candida glabrata and C. auris are listed spectrum exceptions, and glabrata is susceptible dose-dependent to resistant across the azoles. That explains why this ICU patient's candidemia persisted on fluconazole. The echinocandins (micafungin, caspofungin, anidulafungin, rezafungin) are active against Candida including glabrata and are used for invasive candidiasis.

Echinocandins inhibit beta-1,3-glucan synthase, blocking a critical component of the fungal cell wall rather than the membrane. They are IV only, distribute widely, and are cleared by the liver, with raised liver enzymes and infusion reactions as adverse effects. She has no meningitis or urinary infection, which matters because echinocandins do not reach the CNS or urine.
why: Polyenes bind ergosterol; inhibiting 14-alpha demethylation of lanosterol is the azole mechanism.
Neuraminidase inhibitors are influenza antivirals with no antifungal activity.
Flucytosine is an antimetabolite that is avoided as monotherapy for any fungus.
Fluconazole already failed against C. glabrata, and binding ergosterol to form pores describes amphotericin, not azoles.
explain.takeaway: Fluconazole does not reliably cover Candida glabrata or auris; echinocandins, which inhibit beta-1,3-glucan synthesis in the cell wall, treat invasive candidiasis from these species.

explain.objective: Describe common uses for agents discussed

questions.stem:
A 31-year-old man with untreated advanced immunodeficiency has 2 weeks of headache, fever, and confusion. Opening pressure on lumbar puncture is high, and an India ink preparation of spinal fluid shows encapsulated budding yeasts. He is started on amphotericin B together with a second drug that is converted inside fungal cells to an antimetabolite. On day 10 his white cell count is 1,900/mm3 (4,500 to 11,000) and platelets 60,000/mm3 (150,000 to 400,000).

Which statement about the second drug is correct?
choices: It is an echinocandin that reaches the spinal fluid well
It inhibits lanosterol demethylation and causes visual hallucinations
It inhibits the viral DNA terminase complex
It is avoided as monotherapy and can suppress the bone marrow
It binds ergosterol and causes potassium wasting

explain.html:
Encapsulated budding yeast on India ink in the spinal fluid of an immunocompromised patient is cryptococcal meningitis, which is treated with amphotericin B plus flucytosine. Flucytosine (5-FC) is an antimetabolite active against Candida and Cryptococcus and is the one systemic antifungal that does not target the membrane or cell wall. It is typically avoided as monotherapy for any fungus.

Its adverse effects are GI upset, leukopenia and thrombocytopenia, hepatotoxicity, aplastic anemia and photosensitivity, and marrow suppression is worse with zidovudine or ganciclovir. This patient's falling white cell and platelet counts on day 10 fit flucytosine marrow toxicity. Check counts regularly during combination therapy.
explain.table:
Systemic antifungalTargetSignature toxicity
Amphotericin BBinds ergosterol (membrane)Nephrotoxicity, low potassium and magnesium
AzolesErgosterol synthesis (lanosterol demethylation)Liver enzymes, QTc; CYP3A4 interactions
EchinocandinsBeta-1,3-glucan (cell wall)Liver enzymes, infusion reactions
FlucytosineAntimetaboliteLeukopenia, thrombocytopenia, aplastic anemia
why: Echinocandins do not penetrate the CNS, and the second drug here is an antimetabolite, not a cell wall agent.
Lanosterol demethylase inhibition with visual hallucinations describes voriconazole, not the drug paired with amphotericin.
Terminase inhibition is the mechanism of letermovir, a CMV drug.
Binding ergosterol with potassium wasting describes amphotericin B, the first drug, not the second.
explain.takeaway: Cryptococcal meningitis is treated with amphotericin B plus flucytosine, an antimetabolite avoided as monotherapy that causes leukopenia and thrombocytopenia.
